abstracts.value: We explore the sense in which the state of a physical system may or may not be regarded (an) observable in quantum mechanics. Simple and general arguments from various lines of approach are reviewed which demonstrate the following no-go claims: (1) the structure of quantum mechanics precludes the determination of the state of a single system by means of measurements performed on that system only; (2) there is no way of using entangled two-particle states to transmit superluminal signals. Employing the representation of observables as general positive operator valued measures, our analysis allows one to indicate whether optimal separation of different states is achieved by means of sharp or unsharp observables.

We explore the sense in which the state of a physical system may or may not be regarded (an) observable in quantum mechanics. Simple and general arguments from various lines of approach are reviewed which demonstrate the following no-go claims: (1) the structure of quantum mechanics precludes the determination of the state of a single system by means of measurements performed on that system only; (2) there is no way of using entangled two-particle states to transmit superluminal signals. Employing the representation of observables as general positive operator valued measures, our analysis allows one to indicate whether optimal separation of different states is achieved by means of sharp or unsharp observables.
